draftNote: Draft — the hieroglyphs are read from the printed type of Budge's 1895 edition of the papyrus, and the signs and readings are still being checked; expect changes.
sourceStatement: Papyrus of Ani (British Museum EA 10470), {plates}. Hieroglyphs transcribed from the interlinear text of E. A. W. Budge, The Book of the Dead: The Papyrus of Ani in the British Museum (London, 1895), {cite}; Budge's transliteration and word-by-word English were used to check the reading of the signs and the sense, never for wording. Only the papyrus's own text is given: the passages Budge supplies from other papyri in his appendixes and footnotes are left out. Transliteration in the Leiden convention, with the reed written i; translation made fresh from the Egyptian. Shown left to right; the papyrus is written in columns read from the top down. The line under each word ("say") is the conventional Egyptological classroom pronunciation — a neutral e between consonants; ꜣ and ꜥ as a; w as u or w; ṯ as tj; ḏ as dj; ḫ and ẖ as kh; š as sh — an artificial teaching pronunciation, since the vowels of Egyptian were never written. The grouping of signs within a word follows Budge's type, which regularises the scribe's hand.
supplementSourceStatement: A supplement to the Papyrus of Ani, which does not have this passage. In other papyri of the Theban Book of the Dead, Spell 125 continues after the 42 declarations with this address to the gods; {witness}. Hieroglyphs transcribed from the Appendix that E. A. W. Budge prints at this point in The Book of the Dead: The Papyrus of Ani in the British Museum (London, 1895), {cite}; his transliteration and word-by-word English were used to check the reading of the signs and the sense, never for wording. Transliteration in the Leiden convention, with the reed written i; translation made fresh from the Egyptian. The line under each word ("say") is the conventional Egyptological classroom pronunciation, an artificial teaching pronunciation. The grouping of signs within a word follows Budge's type.
